intro: Mission Zero. Give it a goal. Let it discover the path. Demand proof.
goal: The goal: in the Verizon 2025 Data Breach Investigations Report, how many confirmed breaches were analyzed, and what share involved the human element? Mission Zero has no plan and no answer. Public sources only, no spending.
turns: Turn one. A hypothesis, then a web search. It finds the report: a 117-page PDF. The evaluator is strict: three out of ten. It pivots.
Turn two. It reads the whole PDF and keeps only the passages that match what it is looking for. Still not enough: score two. The lesson is stored.
Turn three. A new search confirms twelve thousand one hundred ninety-five breaches, but not the human element. Five out of ten.
Turn four. Back to the PDF with a sharper question: the human element. Both figures have now been seen in the report itself.
draft: The writer drafts an answer from what was seen. A page that was never read cannot be cited.
verify: The verifier re-reads each cited page and demands an exact quote. Green means the page really says it. A red claim caps the score at five.
contradict: A contradictor attacks the answer, a judge scores it, and only the best version is kept. This time: no flaw found, nothing to rewrite.
result: Twelve thousand one hundred ninety-five confirmed breaches. Sixty percent human element. Judge: ten out of ten. Two green proofs. Total cost: six cents.
outro: Built during the hackathon on Meta Muse Spark, with reasoning effort tuned per role: a mission costs a few cents. Everything is in the repository. Mission Zero: proof, not promises.
